tracks.tagline: Wrap a real third-party API into a small internal tool for a 'client', complete with a config-driven dashboard, runbook docs, and handling for the messy edge cases real integrations hit.

1.title: Wrapping a Third-Party API
1.goal: Pick a real public API (weather, currency exchange, GitHub, or similar) and build a clean Python wrapper around it, as if you were the engineer a client hired to 'just make this API work for us'. This is the core skill of forward-deployed work: making someone else's API usable and reliable.
learn: Reading third-party API docs and identifying auth requirements and rate limits
Wrapping raw HTTP calls in a small client class with clear methods
Handling API errors, timeouts and rate limits gracefully
Keeping API keys out of code with `.env` and `python-dotenv`
steps: Pick a free public API with clear docs (OpenWeatherMap, exchangerate.host, or the GitHub REST API) and sign up for a key if one is required.
Create a project folder, install `requests` and `python-dotenv`, and store any key in a `.env` file added to `.gitignore` before your first commit.
Write an `ApiClient` class with one method per useful operation (e.g. `get_current_weather(city)`, `get_forecast(city, days)`), each returning clean Python dicts, not raw response objects.
Wrap every request in `try`/`except` handling network errors, non-200 status codes, and JSON decode errors, raising a custom `ApiClientError` with a clear message.
Add basic retry logic (2 retries with a short delay) for transient failures like timeouts or 5xx responses.
Write a small CLI script that calls 2-3 client methods with real inputs and prints the results, to prove the wrapper works end to end.
Test at least one deliberate failure case (invalid city name, bad API key) and confirm your client raises `ApiClientError` instead of crashing with a raw traceback.
Commit your code (not `.env`) with a README on how to get a key, install dependencies, and run the CLI.
deliverables: An `ApiClient` class wrapping at least 2 real endpoints of a chosen third-party API
Custom error handling with a clear `ApiClientError` for failures
Basic retry logic for transient errors
A CLI script proving the client works against the live API
done_when: Calling each client method with valid input returns clean, correctly-typed Python data
A deliberately invalid input (bad city, bad symbol) raises `ApiClientError` with a readable message, not a raw traceback
The API key never appears anywhere in committed code or Git history
The CLI script runs successfully end to end against the live API
hints: Read the rate-limit section of your chosen API's docs first — free tiers often cap you at 60 requests/minute or less, which affects how you test.
Keep the wrapper's public methods returning plain dicts or small dataclasses, not the `requests.Response` object, so the rest of your code never touches raw HTTP details.
[OpenWeatherMap's API docs](https://openweathermap.org/api) and [exchangerate.host docs](https://exchangerate.host/#/docs) both have a free tier with no credit card needed.
1.stretch: Add response caching (an in-memory dict keyed by request params, with a 5-minute expiry) to avoid hitting rate limits during repeated testing.
post_highlights: Built a clean Python wrapper around a real third-party API with proper error handling
Added retry logic for transient network failures in an API client
Learned to turn a raw external API into a reliable internal tool

2.title: Config-Driven Dashboard for a 'Client'
2.goal: Turn last week's API wrapper into a small internal dashboard for an imagined client, where what's shown is driven by a config file rather than hardcoded — because real clients always want to add or change tracked items without you editing code every time.
learn: Designing a simple config file format (JSON or YAML) to drive an app's behaviour
Building a lightweight dashboard UI with Streamlit
Separating configuration from code so non-engineers could plausibly edit it
Displaying live data pulled through your Week 1 API client
steps: Invent a realistic client scenario (e.g. 'TravelCo tracks weather for 5 client cities' or 'FxDesk tracks 5 currency pairs') and write it down in one paragraph.
Design a `config.json` (or `.yaml`) listing the tracked items (city names, currency pairs) plus a couple of display preferences (units, refresh interval).
Write a `load_config(path)` function that validates the config has the required keys and raises a clear error naming the missing key if not.
Install Streamlit and build `app.py` that reads the config, calls your Week 1 `ApiClient` for each tracked item, and displays results in a table or set of cards.
Add a manual 'Refresh data' button that re-fetches from the live API, and show a 'last updated' timestamp.
Handle the case where one tracked item fails (e.g. a typo'd city name) by showing an inline error for that row while the rest of the dashboard still renders.
Test the dashboard with a config containing one deliberately broken entry and confirm the rest of the dashboard still works.
Commit your code with an updated README explaining the config file format with an example.
deliverables: A `config.json`/`config.yaml` describing tracked items for a fictional client
A `load_config` function with clear validation errors
A Streamlit dashboard showing live data per config entry with a manual refresh
Graceful per-row error handling for one bad config entry
done_when: Editing `config.json` to add or remove a tracked item changes the dashboard without any code changes
The dashboard clearly shows when data was last refreshed
A config with one invalid entry (bad city/symbol) still renders the dashboard for the valid entries, with a visible error for the bad one
Running `load_config` on a config missing a required key raises a clear, specific error
hints: Keep the config schema small (5-8 fields) at first; it's easier to add fields later than to redesign a bloated schema.
Streamlit reruns the whole script on every interaction, so keep the config load and API calls cheap, or cache them with `st.cache_data`.
The [Streamlit documentation](https://docs.streamlit.io) has a caching guide and layout examples (columns, metrics) useful for a dashboard like this.
2.stretch: Add a config field for a per-item alert threshold (e.g. temperature above X, exchange rate above Y) and highlight rows that cross it.
post_highlights: Built a config-driven internal dashboard so a client could add tracked items without code changes
Designed a validated config file format for a small internal tool
Handled partial failures gracefully so one bad config entry didn't break the whole dashboard

3.title: Edge Cases, Support Scenarios and Logging
3.goal: Simulate the messy reality of supporting a live integration: rate limits, partial outages, malformed client configs, and a support ticket asking 'why is this wrong?'. This week is about building the resilience and observability that separates a demo from something a client can actually depend on.
learn: Simulating and handling rate-limit and outage scenarios
Structured logging for debugging a live integration after the fact
Writing a support-style root-cause investigation from logs alone
Defensive config validation against realistic client mistakes
steps: Add structured logging (Python's `logging` module) to your API client and dashboard: log every request made, its duration, and its outcome (success/error/rate-limited) to a `app.log` file.

Simulate a rate limit by adding a `--simulate-rate-limit` flag or env var that makes your API client randomly return a fake 429 response some percentage of the time, and handle it with a backoff-and-retry.
Simulate a partial outage: make one tracked item's API call always fail for a stretch of time, and confirm the dashboard degrades gracefully (shows stale/cached data with a warning, not a crash).
Add at least 3 more realistic config validation checks (duplicate entries, an item type your API doesn't support, an out-of-range preference value) with clear error messages.

Write 3 fictional 'client support tickets' describing symptoms (e.g. 'the dashboard showed the wrong currency rate at 3pm yesterday') and, using only your `app.log`, write a short root-cause note for each.
Add a `/health` or `Diagnostics` view (CLI command or dashboard tab) that reports current API reachability, last successful fetch time per item, and recent error counts.
Fix at least one real bug or gap you find while writing the support-ticket investigations.
Commit your code with an updated README documenting the logging format and the diagnostics view.
deliverables: Structured request/error logging across the API client and dashboard
Graceful degradation during a simulated partial outage
3 written root-cause investigations based only on log evidence
A diagnostics view reporting API health and recent errors
done_when: Running with rate-limit simulation on shows retries in the log and the app still completes successfully
A simulated outage on one item shows a clear 'stale data' warning in the dashboard rather than a crash
All 3 support-ticket root-cause notes correctly identify the actual injected cause using only the logs
The diagnostics view accurately reflects a deliberately broken item's status
hints: Log at INFO for normal requests and WARNING/ERROR for retries and failures, so `grep`-ing the log file for 'ERROR' surfaces real problems fast.
When simulating an outage, make it deterministic (e.g. always fail for 'Paris' for the first 20 seconds) so your root-cause notes can be checked against a known ground truth.
Real support work is 80% reading logs carefully — resist the urge to guess the cause before checking the timestamps and error messages.
3.stretch: Add a simple alerting rule: if an item has been failing for more than N minutes, write a highlighted line to a separate `alerts.log`.
post_highlights: Simulated rate limits and partial outages to test an integration's resilience
Added structured logging and a diagnostics view for debugging a live client tool
Practiced support-style root-cause investigation using only application logs

4.title: Setup Docs, Runbook and Client Handoff
4.goal: Package the whole integration the way you'd actually hand it to a client team: clear setup docs, a runbook for common issues, and a short demo. This week is entirely about the documentation and polish that make forward-deployed work usable by people who didn't build it.
learn: Writing setup documentation for a non-engineer or junior engineer audience
Writing an operational runbook: common issues, symptoms, and fixes
Structuring a handoff so someone else could operate the tool without you
Presenting a technical integration clearly to a non-technical stakeholder
steps: Write a `SETUP.md` with numbered steps to get the dashboard running from a clean machine: dependencies, getting an API key, filling in `.env` and `config.json`, and starting the app.
Have someone unfamiliar with your project (a classmate, or yourself after a day away) follow `SETUP.md` exactly and note every point of confusion.
Fix at least 2 real gaps found during that walkthrough (a missing step, an unclear instruction, a wrong assumption).
Write a `RUNBOOK.md` covering at least 5 realistic issues (rate limited, one tracked item down, bad config entry, stale data, dashboard won't start), each with symptoms, likely cause, and fix steps.
Add a `CHANGELOG.md` or 'known limitations' section listing what the tool does not handle yet, so a client team has honest expectations.
Write a one-page 'client summary' (non-technical) explaining what the tool does, what data it shows, and how to ask for changes via the config file.
Record a 2-3 minute demo video walking through the dashboard, one simulated failure from the runbook, and how you'd diagnose it live.
Do a final pass on the whole repo: consistent naming, a top-level README linking to `SETUP.md` and `RUNBOOK.md`, and no leftover debug prints or dead code.
deliverables: A `SETUP.md` verified by an outside walkthrough with fixes applied
A `RUNBOOK.md` covering at least 5 realistic operational issues
A known-limitations section and a one-page non-technical client summary
A 2-3 minute demo video showing the dashboard and a live runbook scenario
done_when: Someone unfamiliar with the project can get the dashboard running using only `SETUP.md`
`RUNBOOK.md` has at least 5 issues each with symptom, cause and fix
The client summary is understandable without any code or API knowledge
The demo video shows one real failure scenario being diagnosed using the runbook
hints: Write `SETUP.md` by literally running the steps yourself on paper first — commands you 'just know' from memory are exactly the ones that go missing.
A good runbook entry reads like: 'Symptom: dashboard shows stale timestamp for one row. Likely cause: that item's API call is failing. Fix: check `app.log` for ERROR lines matching that item's name.'
Keep the client summary to one page and free of jargon; if you can't explain a feature in one plain sentence, the feature or the explanation needs work.
4.stretch: Turn `RUNBOOK.md` into an interactive checklist inside the dashboard itself (a 'Troubleshooting' tab listing the same issues and fixes).
post_highlights: Wrote setup docs and a runbook that let someone else operate my integration without me
Validated my own onboarding docs with a real outside walkthrough and fixed the gaps found
Presented a technical client integration clearly to a non-technical audience
